detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Ioane was the leader of the Syrian mission in Georgia. While his disciples dispersed across Kartli and Kakheti, he chose the forested ridge of Mount Zadeni across from Mtskheta. The site was not empty: it had previously held a sanctuary of Zaden, the Iberian pagan god of fertility. Setting up a Christian hermitage on top of the old shrine was a gesture at once practical and fairly blunt.

Daily life on the mountain proved difficult: there was no water on the crest, while bears in the surrounding woods were plentiful. Medieval vitae recount that after Ioane prayed, the animals stopped troubling pilgrims and walked calmly past his cell. The second concern was more earthly still: even a hermit cannot last long on a dry ridge without water. According to tradition, his prayers brought forth a cold spring near the cell—locals hold that its water helps with eye ailments.

Ioane spent the rest of his life here. He was buried in his own cell, and his tomb lies in the northern aisle of the basilica, a few steps from that spring. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Ioane of Zedazeni and the founder of Georgian monasticism.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: In the 8th century, under Catholicos Clement, the small 6th-century stone cell was rebuilt into a three-nave basilica. The older structure was not demolished, but carefully folded into the new building: the northern aisle incorporates the 6th–7th-century chapel containing Ioane's tomb and the rock-cut water basin. Outside, remains of fortification walls and terraces survive—from this height it was convenient not only to live in seclusion, but also to keep an eye on the confluence of the Aragvi and Mtkvari rivers.

Zedazeni is an active men's monastery within the Saguramo reserve. The road climbs through beech and oak forest and emerges onto a stone terrace overlooking Jvari Monastery and the valley of the two rivers.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Of those who headed east into Kakheti, Stephane went farthest toward the frontier. He settled on the slopes below present-day Signagi, near the Khirsa stream, at the eastern edge of the kingdom—a borderland regularly exposed to raids from the mountains and neighboring Caucasian Albania. Rather than retreating to an inaccessible cave, he founded an open missionary community dedicated to St. Stephen the Protomartyr right among the border villages.

According to local church tradition, the monastery carried Archdeacon Stephen's name not merely out of devotion: a relic—his finger—was kept near the altar, turning this frontier outpost into a noted pilgrimage site. Tradition also attributes a spring near the ravine to Stephane's prayers; in an unsettled borderland, water on higher ground sustained villagers whenever siege cut off the lower valley.

Stephane was buried in the 6th-century basilica he founded. The church was rebuilt more than once, yet his raised stone tomb beside the northern wall near the sanctuary was carefully preserved each time. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Stephane of Khirsa.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: The cathedral's architecture consists of several periods stacked one upon another. Stephane's 6th-century three-nave basilica was converted in the 10th century, under Kings Leon and Kvirike the Great, into a domed church, and repaired in the 16th century by King Levan of Kakheti after earthquakes and raids. Asomtavruli inscriptions survive on the facade and in the apse (one is linked to King Kvirike III), while a heavy stone wall encloses the grounds: in this corner of Kakheti, a monastery had to rely on masonry as well as prayer.
Khirsa is an active men's monastery among vineyards below Signagi. Set slightly off the main tourist routes, its courtyard and Stephane's tomb are usually quiet.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: While most of his companions sought quiet in the mountains and gorges, Abibos took on a far more public and risky role as Bishop of Nekresi in Kakheti. In the 6th century Sasanian Persian influence was strong here, and Zoroastrian fire temples stood alongside Christian parishes. Abibos did not avoid confrontation: he traveled through the eastern highlands, preaching and openly challenging Persian religious authority.

Medieval hagiography recounts that Abibos walked into a fire temple and poured water over the brazier, putting out the sacred flame—an argument that left little room for theological debate. Another local tradition links Nekresi with a later raid: villagers are said to have slaughtered pigs and scattered the blood around the gates, after which Muslim attackers chose not to enter. By this tradition, Nekresi is the one monastic complex in Georgia where pork is permitted at the festive table.

Extinguishing the fire was treated by Persian authorities as an offense against the state. Abibos was arrested, beaten, and marched toward the marzpan in Mtskheta; near the village of Rekha he was stoned to death. Chronicles add that his body was left outside the walls for wild animals, which did not touch it. His relics were later moved to Samtavro in Mtskheta. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as a Hieromartyr and patron of Kakheti.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: Nekresi is not a single church, but a compact medieval ensemble on a wooded ridge above the Alazani Valley. Its oldest building predates Abibos himself: a tiny 4th-century basilica, among the earliest stone churches in Georgia. Around it grew a 6th–7th-century three-church basilica, a 9th-century domed church, the ruins of a two-story bishop's palace, a watchtower, and a marani (wine cellar) with clay qvevri set into the floor.

Nekresi is an active men's monastery. The climb up the ridge is too steep for regular traffic, so visitors leave their cars at the bottom and take a shuttle to the upper terraces overlooking the Alazani plain.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Tadeoz—affectionately known in Georgia as Tate—was in no hurry to leave his teacher. When the other fathers dispersed across the country, he stayed at the foot of Mount Zedazeni to care for the aging Ioane and founded a monastery dedicated to St. Stephen the Protomartyr. That foundation, Stepantsminda, gave him his epithet Stepantsmindeli (unrelated to the northern mountain town of Kazbegi, though the two are regularly confused). Only with Ioane's blessing did he move west into Shida Kartli, preaching around Urbnisi and Kaspi.

In time he left the valley parishes for Mount Tslevi above Kaspi, settling in the wooded limestone gorge of Tetrakhevi ("White Gorge"). According to medieval hagiography, Tadeoz cut a small cell into the rock and lived in silence and prayer. Solitude, as often happened with hermits, proved relative: shepherds and villagers from the surrounding settlements regularly climbed the gorge to ask for his blessing and healing.
Tadeoz lived to old age and was buried in the cave church he founded at Tetrakhevi. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Tadeoz (Thaddeus) of Stepantsminda.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: The Tetrakhevi (Stepantsminda) Fathers' Monastery stands on the forested northern slope of Mount Tslevi near Kaspi. The medieval hall church is built of rough-hewn local stone and tufa directly over the 6th-century rock-cut cell. Sections of earlier masonry and a rock-cut crypt, where the saint's tomb was venerated, survive.
The monastery lies off paved roads and is reached on foot or by off-road vehicle along the wooded slopes above Kaspi.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Zenon sought neither desert nor sheer cliffs: he settled in a valley at the foot of the Gombori range near Telavi. His goal was not extreme austerity, but a stable monastic community able to teach and run its own economy. The calculation proved far-sighted—Ikhalto later became one of the chief centers of learning in medieval Georgia.

In the early 12th century King David the Builder invited the philosopher Arsen Ikaltoeli to turn the monastery into an academy. Students studied theology, astronomy, mathematics, rhetoric, metalworking, and pharmacology—and, judging by the large stone wine presses in the yard, winemaking was pursued with no less diligence. Georgian tradition counts the poet Shota Rustaveli among the academy's students, though no documentary proof exists.

Zenon was buried in the Church of the Transfiguration (Khvtaeba), beneath the southern vault near the altar. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Zenon of Ikhalto; his individual feast day is 30 October (17 October Old Style).

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: Structures from several periods share the grounds at Ikhalto. The oldest is the small 6th-century domed Church of the Holy Spirit (Sameba), which preserves Zenon's cell on its second level. Next to it stands the 8th–9th-century Church of the Transfiguration, built over the earlier basilica holding his grave. Of the 12th-century Academy, stone walls with tall arched windows, a lecture hall, scriptorium niches, a stone wine press (satsnakheli), and buried qvevri remain; the roof was burned in 1616 by the army of Shah Abbas I.
Ikhalto is an active church complex and open historical monument shaded by old cypress trees. Visitors may walk freely through the remains of the academy and the former wine cellars.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Davit began within the bounds of present-day Tbilisi, living in a cave on Mount Mtatsminda—whose name ("Holy Mountain") is linked to him. Proximity to the city did not suit him: with his disciple Lukiane he moved south into the Gareja semi-desert on the modern Georgian-Azerbaijani border. The terrain was treeless and arid, so both shelter and water cisterns had to be cut straight into the sandstone.

Medieval tradition preserves two well-known stories about Davit. In the first, the hermits survived on the milk of wild deer that came to their cave; when a serpent living in the rocks swallowed a fawn, Davit struck it with his staff and lightning destroyed the creature—a scene frequently painted on Georgian frescoes. In the second, Davit walked to Jerusalem, paused on a hill outside the walls, and, judging himself unworthy to enter the city, contented himself with picking up three stones. That night an angel warned the Patriarch of Jerusalem that the monk was carrying off "all the grace of Jerusalem"; messengers caught up with Davit and took back two stones, leaving him one—the "Stone of Grace."

Davit was buried in the cave Church of the Transfiguration at the Lavra. The Stone of Grace was kept there before being moved to Sioni Cathedral in Tbilisi. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Davit of Gareja; the feast of Davitgarejoba is observed on the Thursday after Ascension.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: The David Gareja Lavra is cut into a sandstone cliff face. Around Davit's original 6th-century cleft, monks from the 9th to the 13th century excavated hundreds of cells, refectories with stone benches, bakeries, and chapels. In a waterless steppe, survival depended on engineering no less than asceticism: a network of gutters cut into the tilted rock strata channeled rainwater into deep underground cisterns.

The lower Lavra is an active men's monastery. Some chapels on the upper ridge, including Udabno, lie along a disputed section of the border with Azerbaijan, so access conditions are best checked before visiting.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: After parting with Ioane of Zedazeni, Ioseb moved into northern Kakheti, onto the Alazani plain beneath the wall of the Greater Caucasus. According to tradition, the area was sparsely inhabited and nearby highlanders gathered there for seasonal festivals of a moon deity. Ioseb built a small church dedicated to St. George; hagiography notes that he wore a cross containing a fragment of the True Cross.

Medieval hagiography links the monastery's later rise to a chance encounter on a hunt. A Kakhetian nobleman riding through the thickets of the Alazani plain came upon the solitary monk at prayer; impressed by both the man and his relic, the prince funded the first stone church and enlisted neighboring villages to protect the community. From that modest 6th-century building grew, in the early 11th century, a cathedral that remained the tallest church in Georgia for a long time.

Ioseb was buried in the church he founded, and when the 11th-century cathedral was raised, his tomb was preserved in the northern part of the sanctuary. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Ioseb (Joseph) of Alaverdi; the regional festival of Alaverdoba is held in late September.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: St. George Cathedral was built in the early 11th century by King Kvirike III of Kakheti, incorporating the foundation of the 6th-century church. Rising over 50 meters, it is enclosed by a fortified wall and articulated outside with restrained blind arcades. Inside, after 19th-century whitewash was cleaned away, frescoes of the 11th, 15th, and 16th centuries came to light—among them a Virgin and Child in the apse and a rare portrait of Ioseb above his tomb.

Alaverdi is an active men's monastery and the seat of the Metropolitan of Alaverdi. The monks run a working estate: they tend vineyards and apiaries and ferment wine in a marani dating from the 8th–11th centuries.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Anton's epithet itself explains his temperament: Martqopi comes from marto-mkopi, "the one who lives alone." Together with the other Syrian fathers he brought a famed relic to Georgia—the Anchiskhati, a ceramic tile bearing the Image of Christ Not Made by Hands (Acheiropoieta), linked by tradition to the Mandylion of King Abgar of Edessa. Anton settled in the wooded hills east of Tbilisi.

Hagiographical tradition describes Anton as a stylite. His seclusion was discovered by accident when a royal hunting party came across his tame deer in the woods, and villagers soon began making their way up to him. To keep his vow of silence without turning people away, Anton found a vertical solution: he built a narrow stone tower on a rocky ridge above the monastery and spent the last fifteen years of his life at the top, counseling disciples from above.

After his death, his disciples brought his body down from the pillar and buried him in the main monastery church, beneath the north wall before the icon of the Mother of God. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Anton of Martqopi; his feast day is 29 August, the feast of the Image Not Made by Hands.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: The monastery occupies two levels: the main complex below and Anton's pillar on the wooded ridge above. The 6th-century church where the relic was kept suffered heavily from invasions—above all Timur's campaign of 1395, when the icon was hidden and later moved to Tbilisi (it is now in the Georgian National Museum). The buildings in the lower courtyard date mostly to the 17th–19th centuries, including an 1848 bell tower by architect Kalina. A steep forest trail of about twenty minutes leads up to a reconstructed stone tower on the foundations of the original pillar.
Martqopi is an active men's monastery in the woods just outside Tbilisi. The trail to Anton's tower starts directly from the monastery enclosure.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Unlike the companions who withdrew to forests and deserts, Ise was given administrative work. According to tradition, Catholicos Evlavios and Ioane of Zedazeni ordained him Bishop of Tsilkani and placed him over a royal cathedral on the Mukhrani plain northwest of Mtskheta. He preached and organized parishes across the mountain valleys leading toward the Caucasus range.

The best-known tradition about Ise concerns a decidedly practical trouble: drought. When the fields around Tsilkani began to dry out while the Ksani River flowed at a distance, medieval hagiography recounts that Ise walked down to the bank, touched the water with his bishop's crozier, and ordered it to follow him. Walking back and drawing a line in the earth with his staff, he is said to have led a stream all the way to Tsilkani, starting the village's irrigation canal.

Ise served his see into old age and was buried in the Tsilkani Cathedral of the Mother of God, beneath the floor between the sanctuary and the northern choir. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Ise, Bishop and Wonderworker of Tsilkani; his feast day is 15 December (2 December Old Style).

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: The church at Tsilkani is older than Ise himself: it was founded in the 4th–5th century by King Bakar, son of Mirian III, Georgia's first Christian ruler. In the 5th–6th centuries it was rebuilt as a three-nave basilica and later as a domed cathedral; an 18th-century stone wall with round corner towers surrounds the grounds. Inside, early medieval carved reliefs and a venerated copy of the 9th-century Tsilkani Icon of the Mother of God are preserved.
Tsilkani is an active cathedral and parish church in a village about twenty minutes' drive from Mtskheta. A stone slab marks Bishop Ise's grave.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Shio, called the Cave-Dweller, went west from Mtskheta along the northern bank of the Mtkvari and settled in a narrow limestone gorge, in a cleft in the cliff. His pursuit of solitude produced an unexpected result: word of the hermit spread quickly, and according to chronicles up to two thousand monks gathered in the canyon, forming one of the largest monastic communities in medieval Georgia.

Hagiographies recount that in his early years a dove brought him food, and when the brothers were choosing a site for the first church, Shio burned incense on his bare palm without injury and told them to build where the smoke settled. Later, weary of renown and visits from the nobility, he carried the idea of seclusion to its logical limit: he had a vertical pit (mgvime) about ten meters deep dug into the limestone. Tradition holds that he spent his last fifteen years at the bottom, receiving bread and water in a basket through a narrow opening.

Shio was buried at the bottom of that same pit, which became a crypt for his relics. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Shio the Cave-Dweller (Shio Mgvimeli); his feast is observed on Cheesefare Thursday, before Great Lent.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: Because the monastery grew around a vertical cave in a narrow gorge, its buildings are arranged in tiers along the cliff. The oldest is the 6th-century octagonal domed Church of St. John the Baptist, built partly into the rock beside the mouth of Shio's pit. Above it stands the 11th–12th-century Upper Church (Zemo Eklesia), founded under David the Builder and rebuilt as a brick-and-stone basilica after Persian and Mongol raids. More than a hundred cave cells of the 6th–12th centuries are cut into the limestone wall behind it.
Shio-Mgvime is an active men's monastery a short drive from Mtskheta. Inside the 6th-century church, visitors can see the opening of the pit where Shio lived for fifteen years.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Isidore—called Ezderios in early chronicles—traveled west from Mtskheta into the fertile valley of Shida Kartli and stopped on the left bank of the Lekhura River. He did not withdraw into the wilderness: he founded the Church of the Ascension and a missionary school, making Samtavisi a center of learning and relief for the surrounding farming villages.

The site's greatest artistic renown arrived five hundred years later. In 1030, a local bishop and architect named Hilarion Kansavulidze raised a new cathedral over Isidore's grave. The carving of its eastern facade—a large ornamental cross and a griffin—proved so successful that Georgian builders reproduced the composition for roughly the next two hundred years.
Isidore's tomb lies in Samtavisi Cathedral, on the northern side of the sanctuary. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Isidore (Ezderios) of Samtavisi.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: Nothing of Isidore's 6th-century basilica remains above ground, but the 1030 cross-domed cathedral survives in good condition despite a 15th-century earthquake that brought down its original dome and western wall. On the eastern facade is the carved cross flanked by two diamond-shaped rosettes, with a griffin beneath the central window. Beside the cathedral stand a fortified bishop's residence and a two-story 17th-century bell tower set directly atop the defensive wall.
Samtavisi is an active cathedral and episcopal residence just off the main highway near Kaspi. Seventeenth-century frescoes survive in the apse, and a stone canopy marks Isidore's grave.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Piros settled on the bank of the Dvani River at Breti, near present-day Kareli in Shida Kartli. Medieval hymns call him a "divine image of repentance" for his strict fasting and night vigils, yet he did not shut himself off from people: his monastery served as a refuge for the poor, the sick, and those with nowhere else to turn.

The best-known monument linked to Breti is neither a cave nor a fortress wall, but a work of goldsmithing. In the 11th century, the master Gabriel Sapaneli made a processional cross for the monastery: a wooden core sheathed in chased silver and gold sheets with scenes from the life of Christ and Georgian inscriptions. It survived the raids and is now kept in the Georgian National Museum in Tbilisi.

Piros was buried in the small 6th-century church he built at Breti. When the monastery was later expanded, the original chapel was not torn down, but kept as the northern burial chamber. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Piros of Breti; his feast day is 28 May (15 May Old Style).

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: Breti shows clearly how medieval builders treated earlier shrines: directly south of Piros's small 6th-century hall church, they added the larger 8th–9th-century St. George hall church of yellowish sandstone. Restoration beneath layers of soot and whitewash uncovered fragments of 11th–13th-century frescoes depicting the Church Fathers, along with medieval Georgian graffiti scratched into the plaster by pilgrims.
Breti is a village church and monastic complex set among orchards in the Kareli district. A low doorway leads into Piros's burial chamber.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Mikhail crossed the Likhi range separating eastern and western Georgia and settled in the wooded gorge of the Cheratkhevi River near Surami. There, on a mountain slope beside the old roads linking the two halves of the country, he founded Ulumbo Monastery.

Few early written accounts of Mikhail survive, and for a specific reason: around 1400, Timur's army sacked Ulumbo and burned its library and archives. Memory of the saint rested on oral tradition—local stories of a spring he blessed and of the Ulumbo icon of the Mother of God, which villagers are said to have carried into the forest whenever foreign armies crossed the pass.

Twentieth-century excavations uncovered a tomb directly in front of the altar of the Ulumbo church, matching the long-standing tradition that Mikhail was buried in the chancel of his church. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Mikhail of Ulumbo; his feast is observed on the third day after Ascension.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: The Church of the Assumption of the Mother of God at Ulumbo stands in the woods above the village of Alisiubani. The 6th-century church and its medieval successors were destroyed repeatedly during Timur's invasion and later Ottoman raids. The Amirejibi noble family rebuilt it in the 17th–18th centuries and again in 1871, neatly setting surviving medieval carved reliefs and cornice blocks into the exterior masonry, where they are easy to spot.
Ulumbo is an active monastery in the forest of the Khashuri district, reached by a dirt road running alongside a mountain stream.
